NEW YORK, Oct 15 : Geographically dispersed Games are well on their way to becoming the norm, USOPC CEO Sarah Hirshland said on Thursday, as the growing scale of the Olympics complicates infrastructure plans for hosts. IOC officials hailed the most recent Milano Cortina Games as a success, despite early concerns over the first spread-out Winter Olympics that had venues scattered over 22,000 kilometres.  The upcoming LA28 Games are also expected to be spread out, with softball and canoe slalom set to take place in Oklahoma City and soccer to be in several metropolitan areas: New York City; Columbus, Ohio; Nashville, Tennessee; St. Louis; San Jose, California; and San Diego. "The disbursement of the Games themselves is evolving. And a lot of that is because the scale of the Games has gotten so big and significant that the infrastructure required to host is very hard to find in a single place," said Hirshland, who was speaking from the Columbia University Sports Management Conference.

The 2030 Games in the French Alps are expected to follow the Milano Cortina model, with venues in Nice and the Alpine regions. New York state this year formed an exploratory committee to host the 2042 Winter Games, with the duties to be shared between the five boroughs and Lake Placid.  By comparison, the centralised plan for Utah 2034's venues will serve as a "rare exception," said Hirshland. "It is likely that the LA 2028 Games will be the largest summer Games ever," she said.  "My guess is that the summer Games thereon after will probably be smaller than what we're going to see in LA. And a lot of that is infrastructure demand, cost demand, and to some degree there is a point at which even the logistics get so cumbersome that you can't continue to grow unless you really rethink the way you do it."

Source: Reuters

Oct 15 : Thoma Bravo-owned cybersecurity company Proofpoint will buy data security firm Varonis Systems in all-cash deal valued at about $6.3 billion, the companies said on Thursday. Under the agreement, Varonis shareholders will receive $49.75 per share in cash, representing a premium of 52 per cent over Varonis' closing stock price on June 22, the day before initial speculation about a potential sale, according to the companies. Reuters reported in September that Proofpoint was in discussions to acquire Varonis Systems. Miami-based Varonis offers cybersecurity services, including data classification on cloud storage systems and employee behavior tracking. Its shares were up about 2 per cent in extended trading. Thoma Bravo in 2021 agreed to acquire Proofpoint, which sells software that helps companies guard against cyberattacks, valuing the firm at about $12.3 billion in the take-private deal.

Source: Reuters

Oct 15 : CoreWeave's mounting debt is raising fresh concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centres. Shares and bonds of the Nvidia-backed company have tumbled despite its CEO's assurances of a strong contract backlog, fueling a broader selloff in technology stocks. Here is why investors are worried and what its troubles could mean for the industry. WHAT DOES COREWEAVE DO?

CoreWeave rents out computing power from Nvidia processors to companies developing and running AI, including Microsoft and OpenAI. It is one of the leading "neocloud" providers, a group of newer cloud companies that are growing rapidly to meet demand for scarce and expensive AI chips. These neocloud companies give customers access to computing power without requiring them to build their own data centers. However, supplying such capacity requires heavy upfront investment in chips and infrastructure, often financed with debt. WHAT IS ITS FINANCIAL SITUATION? The company, which has never turned a profit, has about $50 billion in debt, according to data compiled by LSEG. It raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion in August to between $35 billion and $39 billion. Analysts expect revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion. The yields on its bonds due in 2031, which are rated junk, have spiked to about 16 per cent, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to about 1,000 basis points, reflecting growing concern among creditors. CEO Mike Intrator told employees in an internal memo seen by Reuters that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a $104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by more than $25 billion in new commitments early in the third quarter. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also downplayed the concerns, saying CoreWeave's financial strength is improving and he sees no need to backstop it. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 2032. WHY IT COULD BE A CANARY IN THE COAL MINE CoreWeave's business depends on two things: demand for AI computing and lenders' willingness to finance the infrastructure supplying it. But a selloff in its shares suggests a lack of confidence among investors in the latter, even as the company cites strong demand. The concern is not that AI demand will collapse, but that higher borrowing costs could make the business harder to sustain if demand were to weaken sharply. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade's canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. WHY ARE MARKETS FRETTING? Investors are questioning whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover the cost of building and financing the infrastructure. CoreWeave has to spend heavily upfront before it can collect the revenue from its contracts. Higher interest rates could drive up financing costs and further squeeze returns. The hardware itself poses another risk. Chips lose value as newer generations arrive, pushing providers to spend even more to replace them. The concerns, however, go beyond CoreWeave. US technology giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year. THE DOWNSIDE SCENARIO One potential consequence would be a broader financing squeeze, with lenders demanding higher returns or becoming less willing to fund other AI projects. That could force providers to scale back expansion, curbing equipment purchases and affecting the computing capacity customers expect. A setback could also deepen doubts that the AI investment frenzy is outpacing returns, piling further pressure on technology stocks. The impact of the fallout would depend on how the business is reorganized, and CoreWeave's ties to major technology companies do not, by themselves, mean its failure would trigger a wider financial crisis. WHO ELSE BEARS THE RISK? Gartner estimates about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, warning that expected AI revenue will not support profitable returns on all planned infrastructure spending. Neocloud rivals Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren have fallen in the recent selloff. The cost of default protection has risen for SoftBank, which is betting heavily on OpenAI. Meanwhile, spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia have also reached records, although they have risen much more slowly than CoreWeave's. However, these companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Oct 15 : The NFL is developing a tech platform geared toward flag football training, the league's senior vice president for global flag football Brian Flinn said on Thursday, as it continues an aggressive push into the game. The platform will address the training and development gap in the sport, said Flinn, with the non-tackle form of the game seeing a surge in participation ahead of its Olympic debut at LA28. "No one's really done the work to understand how unique the discipline is and what training modules do you need to get athletes ready," said Flinn, appearing at the Columbia University Sports Management Conference. "We're working with third-party experts in that space to develop curriculum so that we can train athletes to go a little bit further.

"And then on the coaching and officiating side, the reality is there's a lot of great people out there, in some cases volunteering their time. And it's not an indictment on them, but the reality is no one's invested in them to develop them to keep up with the demanding players at every level." Flag football has emerged as a key piece of the NFL's global strategy as it included a record nine games in its international schedule this season. The league is chasing millions of fans outside the US, after launching its global markets programme in 2021. The sport is widely perceived as having a lower barrier to entry for newcomers with less risk of injuries commonly seen in the bone-crunching tackle sport, and the NFL views flag as a way of getting more women and girls into its orbit. The NFL earlier this year announced plans to launch a professional flag football league for men and women. "The reality is we need to make more investment in player health and safety," said Flinn. "My expectations in the next three or four months, we'll have a tech platform out there that is training people at scale."

MANCHESTER, England, Oct 15 : Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez apologised on Thursday for criticising the club's hierarchy following their Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, after holding talks with manager Michael Carrick and senior officials. Martinez met with Carrick and club executives after training, two days after saying the club needed greater investment to help the team compete at the highest level following Tuesday's 2-0 loss. "Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager," Martinez said in an Instagram post, in his second statement since the interview. "It was a very positive conversation where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday's game."

A club source said that any internal disciplinary action would remain private, adding that it had been Martinez's decision to apologise publicly and that all parties considered the matter closed. Martinez acknowledged that his frustration following the defeat had got the better of him and apologised for choosing the wrong moment to air his feelings. "Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity," he said. "The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise." The Argentina international had singled out director of football Jason Wilcox in the post-game interview, saying United needed more signings to compete with their rivals and build a squad capable of challenging in Europe. Martinez said his comments had not reflected the unity required at Old Trafford and stressed his belief that everyone at the club was working towards the same goal. "Our club is at its best when we are all united, and I recognise that my words in that moment did not come up with that," he said. "I know that every single person at Manchester United is doing everything possible to achieve our shared ambition, bringing the success that this club and its supporters deserve." Martinez finished his statement by drawing a line under the episode. "With this situation now behind us, we are fully focused on winning together." United are 13th in the Premier League after six games in their worst start in 40 years. They travel to seventh-placed Leeds United on Sunday.

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK: Germany warned on Thursday (Oct 15) against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage, while Britain called for tighter sanctions on Russia n shipping, as questions grow about the strength of US support for Ukraine. Russia n Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers in Bangkok, just over a month after the US had hosted his first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. "I do notice attempts, particularly from the United States ... to bring Russia back onto the international stage," German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil told reporters. "There will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again - not with me, and not with the other Europeans."

RIFT OVER RUSSIA SANCTIONS US Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne said Washington supported Russia's presence, noting that allies had not raised their concerns directly with the US delegation this week. "We think it's really important if you're going to solve a crisis, you need to have open dialogue and open conversation," she told Reuters. "And you can't have ... dialogue, and you can't have resolution to conflict if no one's talking to one another." US President Donald Trump remained committed to bringing about a peaceful end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, she said. British finance minister John Healey called on other nations to tighten sanctions on Russia -linked shipping. "My message to finance ministers here today ... on Ukraine, is to stay the path on tough economic sanctions on Russia , especially a tighter ban on shipping services ... that help ( Russia n President Vladimir) Putin's sanctions-busting shadow fleet to operate," he said. Britain has imposed a series of sanctions on shipping and related services that it believes Russia uses to fund and equip its war on Ukraine.

However, a US official said on Wednesday the Trump administration was considering easing sanctions on these vessels, which have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia , Iran and Venezuela. The differences extend beyond sanctions. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that Europe would retain control of Russia n sovereign assets frozen after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, rejecting any suggestion they could be transferred to a US-supervised vehicle as part of a peace initiative. US President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russia n diesel fuel , a move met with criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans in the US Senate. Trump's envoys told Ukrainian officials last week that the diesel deal was part of an effort to draw Russia back to negotiations after the failure of previous efforts to launch sustained talks to end the war. "It is always useful for talks to take place. But I want to be very clear that these talks must not come at Ukraine's expense, or take place over the heads of the Ukrainian people or President Zelenskyy," Klingbeil said.

EU SEEKS TO RAISE FUNDS FOR UKRAINE The EU has pledged €45 billion (US$50 billion) for Ukraine in 2027, but the country's needs will be much higher and the EU is scrambling to organise financial support from countries such as Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan and Britain. Klingbeil said he was discussing with international partners how to ensure Ukraine's financing, with commitments from Australia and South Korea made during meetings on Thursday. Healey said Britain would provide £17 million (US$23 million) in funding towards repairs for Ukraine's Chornobyl nuclear power plant, which had been damaged by a Russia n drone strike last year, alongside support from the US and France.

Oct 15 (Field Level Media) - Carlos Alcaraz will compete at the ATP 500 Erste Bank Open in Vienna for the first time since 2021 after accepting a wild card invitation. The ATP Tour announced the news on Wednesday. The 23-year-old Alcaraz has had an up-and-down season due to a wrist injury, missing both Wimbledon and the French Open. Still, he has managed three titles, starting with the Australian Open championship, followed by victories in Doha and Tokyo. While Italy's Jannik Sinner is out for the rest of the season due to an injury, a chunk of the Top-10 players are expected in Vienna for the indoor event from Oct. 26-Nov. 1. The field, so far, includes Alexander Zverev of Germany, Russian Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli of Italy and Australia's Alex de Minaur. In 2021, at age 18, Alcaraz reached the semifinals in Vienna, losing to eventual champion Zverev. Alcaraz is ranked No. 3 in the world and is 33-5 on the season. (-Field Level Media)

Oct 15 : FIFA will amend its disciplinary regulations after controversy over its decision to suspend U.S. forward Folarin Balogun’s automatic World Cup ban, the Belgian Football Association (RBFA) said on Thursday after raising the issue with soccer’s governing body. The decision follows criticism of FIFA’s move to suspend Balogun’s automatic one-match ban for a red card, allowing the striker to play against Belgium in their last-16 clash. U.S. President Donald Trump said he had personally asked FIFA President Gianni Infantino to review the sanction, prompting questions about the independence of the disciplinary process. Following Thursday's FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, RBFA president and FIFA Council member Pascale Van Damme said the governing body would revise Article 27 of its Disciplinary Code, which allows the implementation of a disciplinary sanction to be suspended in exceptional circumstances.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 15 : Amazon unveiled two new devices on Thursday for listening to and recording people's information throughout the day to offer calendar reminders and other AI-driven insights under the Bee brand it acquired last year. Frontier is a bracelet and Eclipse is a brick that resembles a portable magnetic charger. Users attach the Eclipse to their smartphones. The devices aggregate information from calendars, apps and other data throughout the day, Amazon said.  The Frontier bracelet costs $75 and the Eclipse $100, Amazon said. "They listen to your whole day," said Amazon devices chief Panos Panay at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference in San Francisco. "It reminds you of the conversations you had, it reminds you of to-dos that you may have had, it tells you that you have some action items that you committed to other people."

The company said users control privacy by deciding when to turn it on and can delete insights or prior conversations as they see fit. Amazon does not store audio.  The company faced criticism after reports in 2019 that thousands of people were listening to conversations people had with its Alexa voice assistant service. It is facing a class action lawsuit over the practice. Amazon has denied any wrongdoing. Bee will retain data for 14 days, though users can extend that by paying for a $12-per-month subscription. The devices can also connect to Alexa+, Amazon's subscription generative AI voice service. Amazon's Bee will face competition in AI wearables, notably Meta's Muse Charm, a pendant using the company's latest agentic AI software, and its eyeglasses with cameras and other sensors. A host of startups have also developed similar devices, designed to record conversations and take action on behalf of users. In recent weeks, Amazon has announced a flurry of new gadgets, part of Panay's effort to attract buyers willing to spend more for higher quality and durability. A slate of tablets Amazon announced last week costs as much as three times more than prior versions, despite slowing global sales of the portable computers. Reuters reported earlier this year that Amazon is considering a return to the smartphone market about a decade after the release of its failed Fire Phone.

Oct 15 : Anthropic has given nonprofit METR employee-level access to its systems and is in talks with others including Hugging Face, as AI companies pitch external evaluators as a way to safely advance the technology without slowing its development. The developer of Claude models is also working with biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio and Accenture's AI business Faculty as evaluators, it said in a blog post on Thursday. Reuters exclusively reported earlier this week that Anthropic and OpenAI had sought significant control over what outside reviewers could publish, concerned that the findings could leak trade secrets. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that talks with Anthropic had evolved recently, with the company becoming more open in negotiations.

A key sticking point between evaluators and AI labs is that information the companies might consider crucial intellectual property can also be relevant to assessing a model's risks, leading to disputes and redactions, a separate person familiar with the discussions told Reuters. Experts have also said the independence of evaluators is a concern, as Anthropic and OpenAI choose who gets to carry out the reviews. The outcome of the talks will help determine how the world scrutinizes a technology that some of its creators warn may be advancing beyond humanity's ability to manage. THE METR TIE-UP Anthropic said on Thursday six employees of METR — or Model Evaluation and Threat Research — have company hardware, office space and access to internal systems roughly equivalent to its risk assessment teams. However, customer data, legally privileged information and model architecture will remain off limits. The company said it cannot veto METR's findings on risks, incidents and practices, but can require narrowly defined redactions. METR can also publicly question those redactions without revealing the withheld information. "In line with our transparency policies, our report will openly describe the scope, access, and other limitations of our work," METR said. The nonprofit had proposed on Wednesday that developers allow private staff interviews, timely publication of assessments and transparency about access limits and redactions. Anthropic said its other evaluator partnerships are at an early stage, with more limited access and publication rights.  The company is developing three tiers of access. Evaluators at the first level will conduct narrowly scoped investigations and need approval to publish. Those at the second will receive more information and can publish without approval, subject to redactions evaluators can publicly challenge. The third, used by METR, provides employee-like access with similar publication rights to the second tier. SecureBio is in the first tier and is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of Anthropic's August risk report, having published a pilot review of the previous report. Anthropic said it would consider expanding SecureBio's access and publication rights after the review. Anthropic also announced last month that it is working on a tie-up with Faculty covering model evaluations, adversarial testing and assessments of whether models behave as intended, among other areas.

ZURICH, Oct 15 : Gianni Infantino apologised to the FIFA Council on Thursday, but English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced he was fit to continue as president of soccer's world governing body. Infantino said he had apologised during the closed meeting for mistakes in communicating and consulting over the now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project, but stressed that it had been only a proposal and “in no way a done deal”. "First of all, I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which then led to many consequences," Infantino said in a video published by FIFA.  "But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal, so in no way a done deal."

The FFE plan involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and selling a minority stake to private investors. Infantino said it was intended to generate additional funding for FIFA’s 211 member associations. While Infantino appeared to retain strong support among African officials, opposition from some of Europe’s most influential football associations remained pronounced. German FA president Bernd Neuendorf called for a "complete restart" at FIFA, saying the governance reforms the organisation needed could not be delivered with Infantino in charge. "The first thing is we need reforms. That's true. And everyone knows that," Neuendorf said. "The old administration has to be reformed, and the whole governance has to be reformed. But I'm pretty clear here in this that this is not possible with Gianni. "So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart." English FA chair Debbie Hewitt said Infantino needed to provide answers to questions raised by FIFA Council members and warned that failure to do so would make him unfit to remain president. "I think the man has to answer those questions," Hewitt said. "And if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president." Neuendorf questioned the extent of Infantino’s apology, saying he believed it related primarily to the failure to consult the council rather than to the FFE project itself. "I didn't have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total," Neuendorf said. "My impression was it was just because it wasn't brought forward to the council and no one was involved." Neuendorf said council members had learned about the project through the media rather than from FIFA's leadership and that representatives from other confederations had also complained about the lack of consultation. "When it came to the FFE project as such, I have the impression that this still was not included when he apologised," he said. QUESTIONS UNANSWERED Hewitt said Infantino’s apparent regret over not consulting the council strengthened the case for releasing the relevant FFE documents to its members. "You have an obligation. We all have an obligation, a fiduciary responsibility to answer the questions that have been put forward," Hewitt said. "He told us to submit those questions. There were so many of them, and now it's up to him to do that and do that in the open way. "If there's nothing to hide, then share (the FFE documents) with us... if you regret it that deeply, please share it with us." The meeting also dealt with calls for reform at FIFA, but Hewitt said meaningful changes could not be made until members understood how the decisions at the centre of recent controversies had been reached. She cited FFE, the decision to suspend the automatic one-match ban imposed on United States forward Folarin Balogun after his World Cup red card, and the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to US President Donald Trump as issues requiring greater scrutiny. "Unless we understand what happened, either it was a massive failing in governance because it wasn't followed or actually the governance was followed, but there was something else that got to what we all felt in there was the wrong decisions," Hewitt said. "So we must understand what happened in order to be able to review it. Otherwise we're guessing." The criticism, however, was not unanimous. Ahmed Yahya, the president of the Football Federation of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania (FFRIM), defended Infantino, saying his leadership had helped develop football around the world, pointing to increased funding for national associations and the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams. "We (the African nations) believe Gianni is the right person to continue leading football," Yahya said.  Asked whether most people wanted Infantino to remain president, he added: "I'm certain. The majority want Gianni to stay."

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK: The Nasdaq fell to near one-month lows on Thursday (Oct 15), weighed by a worsening selloff in AI-linked stocks on fears rising interest rates could impact artificial-intelligence investments, and fresh data pointing to building US price pressures. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq marked their biggest one-day fall since July on Wednesday after hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data fuelled expectations of further interest- rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve, dragging on tech stocks. S emiconductor maker TSMC 's cautious note for 2027, citing macroeconomic uncert ai nties, also dented sentiment. Reports that AI lab Anthropic' s third-quarter revenue surged 45 per cent compared to the previous quarter failed to lift investor spirits.

Heavily indebted data-centre operator CoreWeave sitting in the eye of the recent tech storm, lost 8.5 per cent fol low ing a 15 per cent drop on Wednesday , while c loud computing giant Oracle was down marginally after a near ly 9 per cent fall in the previous session. The companies' bonds also fell, pushing their yields to record highs. Chipmakers lost ground, with Nvidia down 3.3 per cent, and Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices losing 5 per cent and 6.4 per cent, respectively. The broader chips index will have shed US$2 trillion in a more-than-14 per cent slide in seven sessions, if losses hold. It would mark its longest losing streak since May 2025. The S&P 500 information technology sector was the biggest drag, down 2 per cent. The slump pushed investors to government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield at a three-week low of 5.0725 per cent. " Investors are increasingly questioning how much future growth is already priced into valuations, how expansion is being financed and when these investments will generate sufficient returns," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note. "The repricing of CoreWeave's debt suggests that investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost."

At 9:50am ET (11:50pm, Singapore time), the Dow J one s Industrial Average rose 163.58 points, or 0.32 per cent, to 51,785.06, the S&P 500 shed 32 .20 points, or 0.42 per cent, to 7,686.74, and the Nasdaq Composite .IXIC lost 283.07 points, or 1.06 per cent, to 26,409.80. The CBOE Volatility Index, known as Wall Street's fear gauge, hit a two-week high and was last up 0.83 points at 17.74. Investors continued to segue into traditionally defensive sectors, with healthcare .SPXHC and consumer staples .SPLRCS rising more than 2 per cent each. Gains in these stocks propped up the Dow. The Nasdaq has dropped more than 4 per cent from record highs touched last week, with concerns about higher borrowing costs and AI spending threatening to eclipse the third-quarter earnings season, when S&P 500 profits are expected to grow 30.6 per cent, according to LSEG data. Data showed US producer prices increased by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising goods and services costs, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products. Markets will now scrutinize Fed Ch ai r Kevin Warsh's speech before the International M one tary Fund Annual Meeting. Shares of Rocket Lab dropped 1 5 per cent after the space company s ai d the inaugural launch of its new, larger Neutron rocket was delayed until next year. FMC slid over 38 per cent after the agrichemicals company sharply cut its third-quarter outlook, which includes a US$625 million-US$675 million hit from commercial actions. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.78-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.05-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 20 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 29 new highs and 261 new lows.

WASHINGTON, Oct 15 : Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project. The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, the report added.  The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post. Reuters has not verified the report. The White House said it would not release information about the donors, who spokesman Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies."

"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," Ingle told Reuters. Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said. Apple declined to comment. The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who say they raise questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms. "The secrecy is a huge problem," said Eric Petry of the Brennan Center for Justice. "When people with business before the government can give millions to the president's pet project, and the public can't see who or how much, there's no way to tell whether they're buying access or favors." Federal contractors including Lockheed Martin Corp, Microsoft Corp and Palantir Technologies Inc all gave $10 million, the Post reported. The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility. The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term. The planned ballroom is among several projects Trump is pursuing in his efforts to remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab. The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful." The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure. Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

Bones from Iraqi cave hint at violence and compassion in Neanderthals

The entrance to Shanidar Cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region, a site of important Neanderthal remains, is seen in an undated photograph released on October 15, 2026. Prof Graeme Barker/Handout via REUTERS NO RESALES. NO ARCHIVES. THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY

Oct 15 : The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care. Researchers have discovered at Shanidar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Neanderthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch (15 mm) wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab. The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet (7.5 meters) of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A's sex. The researchers said the injury's shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source.

"The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung," said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports. "The location could be like the kind of 'heart shot' hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative. We do see heart shots as a hunting strategy both today and in the archaeological record. Neanderthals would have known this would lead to a quick death," Pomeroy said. University of Cambridge archaeologist and study co-author Graeme Barker, who has led Shanidar Cave excavations since 2015, said the likeliest scenario is interpersonal violence. The researchers said the violence probably occurred either between members of a particular Neanderthal group or between members of rival Neanderthal groups, calling a Homo sapiens attack or an accidental injury less likely. The researchers found shards of bone displaced by the weapon. The injury indicated that the spear entered from above with a downward trajectory, penetrating the left chest cavity from the front and traveling through the body before punching the hole in the scapula, causing quick death. ANOTHER INJURY In addition to the scapula, the researchers found some ribs, a nearly complete right hand and seven teeth, mostly from the front of the lower jaw, belonging to Shanidar A. The teeth bore evidence that this Neanderthal had survived brutal injury at least a year before death — a blow to the face resulting in front teeth being smashed and lost. One tooth was split, with half remaining rotated in the mouth and others pushed out of position. "The pain would have been extreme, and basic needs like eating and drinking would have been difficult, perhaps meaning Shanidar A needed food mashing and being able to rest. It's likely that Shanidar A did need some care from members of the group for some basic needs during recovery," Pomeroy said. Shanidar A was one of five Neanderthals, four adults and one infant, whose bodies were carefully tucked behind a rock pillar in the cave in a burial cluster within a generation or so of each other. The cave was occupied by Neanderthals for tens of thousands of years as a seasonal campsite, and later by Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were more robustly built than Homo sapiens, with larger brows. They lived as hunter-gatherers and inhabited Eurasia from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains from about 400,000 years ago until a bit after 40,000 years ago, disappearing after Homo sapiens became established in the region. The two species interbred, with modern non-African human populations bearing residual Neanderthal DNA. The cave, overlooking the Great Zab river valley, has been a source of information about Neanderthals since the 1950s, with Shanidar A now offering new insight into their behavior. "We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature – care and violence – juxtaposed in the same individual," Pomeroy said. "We see evidence all around us today that violence and care are both aspects of how we humans behave, and we see this here in Shanidar A, too. Neanderthals were like us in many respects, both the good and the bad, and this find really highlights that, going against stereotypes of Neanderthals as unintelligent, uncaring cavemen and cavewomen," Pomeroy said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump scrapped plans to livestream the execution of the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, overruling Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Thursday (Oct 15) after the proposal drew opposition from Republicans, religious leaders and the public. The reversal ended a plan to broadcast Nidal Hasan’s Dec 3 firing-squad execution. It also marked a rare public disagreement between Trump and one of the president’s closest allies, although the Pentagon said the two were “completely aligned.” Hegseth had announced plans to livestream the execution at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, the site of Hasan's 2009 attack. No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions. Trump and his advisers had been unaware of the livestream plan, said a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote in a social media post. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." The families of Hasan's victims will be able to view the execution in person if they so choose, as is standard at US executions. Some of Trump 's fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders had expressed everything from doubts to outright condemnation of the Pentagon's livestream plan. Opinion polls showed a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, also raised objections, while Pope Leo condemned capital punishment in all its forms. An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment, and it was unclear if the scheduled Dec 3 execution date would be delayed by legal challenges.

A SPLIT WITH HEGSETH It was Trump 's first major public split with Hegseth, a Trump ally. But it was unclear whether the split would politically imperil Hegseth given their strong ties. In a statement, the Pentagon said Trump spoke with Hegseth about the decision before announcing it on Truth Social. "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. Capital punishment in the US already was facing renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived two lethal injections in a failed execution attempt by Tennessee last month that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalisation.

"SERIOUS CONSEQUENCES" A military jury convicted Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, of premeditated murder for fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast base. Law enforcement shot Hasan during his rampage, paralyzing him from the waist down, and he now uses a wheelchair. Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that "there's serious consequences for these types of things." Midterm elections on Nov 3 will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress as voters increasingly register disapproval of Trump 's policies in opinion polls. Senator John Curtis, a Republican representing Utah, called the cancellation "the right move" in a statement. US Representative Richard Neal, a Democrat from Massachusetts, called the original plan "a profound failure of moral judgment and basic human decency."
